text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes treatment involves lifestyle adjustments, regular blood sugar monitoring, medications, and weight-loss or surgical options when needed.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle adjustments, regular blood sugar monitoring, medications, and weight-loss or surgical options when needed

list.snippet: Healthy eating: Focus on lean proteins, non-starchy vegetables, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats while limiting processed foods and added sugars.
Physical activity: Aim for at least 150 minutes of aerobic and strength exercise per week to improve insulin sensitivity and lower blood sugar.
Weight management: Losing 5% or more of body weight helps improve blood sugar control and reduce health risks.
Blood sugar tracking: Monitor glucose levels regularly using a home glucometer or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) as guided by a healthcare provider.
Metformin: Often prescribed as the first-line oral medication to decrease glucose production in the liver and improve insulin sensitivity.
SGLT2 inhibitors: Oral medications that help the kidneys remove excess sugar through urine while offering heart and kidney benefits.
GLP-1 receptor agonists and GIP/GLP-1 agonists: Injectable (or select oral) medications that lower blood sugar, slow digestion, and support weight loss.
Sulfonylureas and meglitinides: Oral drugs that stimulate the pancreas to produce more insulin.
DPP-4 inhibitors: Oral medications that help keep blood sugar down without causing weight gain or low blood sugar risks.
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): Oral medications that improve insulin sensitivity in muscle, fat, and liver tissue.
Insulin therapy: Synthetic insulin given via pens, syringes, or pumps when other medications no longer keep blood sugar levels in a safe range.
Bariatric (weight-loss) surgery: An option for qualifying body mass index (BMI) levels that can significantly improve or even induce remission of type 2 diabetes.

text_blocks.snippet: For detailed clinical guidance, explore the Mayo Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide, review medication breakdowns on the American Diabetes Association Medication Page, or read the PubMed Central Clinical Review on Early Management.
